title: What is behind the raid on Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar?
text:
What is behind the raid on Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar?
The FBI’s search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home raises concerns about political interference and could impact Minnesota’s Senate race ahead of the midterm elections.
Rep. Ilhan Omar, Democrat of Minnesota, has long been a thorn in President Donald Trump’s side. She’s a Muslim woman of color, a Somali immigrant, and a founding member of the “Squad” – a tight-knit group of young, outspoken progressives in Congress, most of them women.
Now, following a search of her home Monday in Washington, D.C., by federal agents, Representative Omar is under heightened scrutiny over her immigration history as part of a long-running criminal inquiry. She and her family fled Somalia when she was a child, and her father later brought her to the United States as a refugee. In 2000, in her teens, she became a naturalized U.S. citizen.
Ms. Omar faces questions about the immigration paperwork filed by her late father, including her date of birth, according to reporting from The New York Times and The Washington Post. If it turns out that she was already 18 – that is, no longer a minor – when her father filed the citizenship application, she could be “denaturalized” and potentially deported.
The search of a Democratic congresswoman’s home shortly before the midterms raises questions about potential political interference in federal investigations and underscores the Trump administration’s focus on immigration enforcement.
Timing is key in other ways. The raid on her home, just three weeks before the midterm elections, flouts the long-standing Justice Department norm of avoiding major investigative actions against a political candidate within 60 days of an election.
But for President Trump, “norm-busting” has been a defining feature of the second term – from his soaring personal wealth in part through cryptocurrency and real estate ventures to his use of the legal system to pursue perceived enemies.
What are the political implications of this investigation?
Mr. Trump’s immediate concern is the midterm elections on Nov. 3, when his Republican Party faces a potential Democratic “blue wave” and the expected loss of the House and possibly also the Senate. Ms. Omar, now finishing her fourth House term, holds a safe Democratic seat, and the presidential attack isn’t expected to affect the trajectory of that race.
Instead, the impact could be felt in the election in Democratic-leaning Minnesota for an open U.S. Senate seat that isn’t a lock for the Democrats. GOP candidate Michele Tafoya, a retired TV sports reporter, trails Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan by just a few points.
Whether the latest action against Ms. Omar will affect that race is open to debate. But to some analysts, the Trump administration’s effort could backfire and help Democrats.
“It’s not necessarily helpful to Republicans in Minnesota to have this occur just before the election,” says Steven Schier, a professor of political science emeritus at Carleton College in Northfield, Minnesota. “In fact, the less Donald Trump is mentioned in Minnesota, probably the better for Republican candidates.”
Nationally, Mr. Trump’s average job approval rating in polls stands at 37%, similar to polling in Minnesota.
What is the tension between the Trump administration and Representative Omar?
Attacking Ms. Omar has long been a staple of the president’s stump speeches.
On Tuesday, Mr. Trump called Ms. Omar “a terrible person” as he left Washington for campaign appearances around the country. But he declined to take a stand on whether she should be deported. Earlier Monday, at a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio, Mr. Trump said he had “nothing to do with” the search at her home.
Last Saturday, before a crowd in Clarksville, Tennessee, Mr. Trump hinted at possible action against her, saying she came from a country of “crime and squalor.” He also suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Vice President Vance, who is expected to run for president in 2028, said Tuesday that he had no “advance notice” of the Oct. 12 raid on Ms. Omar’s home.
“We try to run our Department of Justice in a fair and honest way. We try to let the law follow the facts rather than creating facts to just prosecute people we don’t like,” Mr. Vance said.
In a post Monday on X, Ms. Omar called the raid “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” She also accused Mr. Trump of targeting her for 10 years “with baseless lies and smear campaigns.”
“I will not be silenced,” Ms. Omar wrote.
Her allies, including both the Democratic National Committee and fellow progressive Pramila Jayapal, a Democratic representative from Washington state, have been sending fundraising emails on her behalf over the search.
Why did Federal agents search Representative Omar’s home?
The Oct. 12 search of Ms. Omar’s Washington home by the Homeland Security Investigations unit of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) was part of a long-running inquiry into her immigration status.
At issue is whether her late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, falsified or omitted information in his application for legal status before becoming a U.S. citizen. If Ms. Omar’s citizenship was obtained inappropriately via her father, her citizenship could be revoked, and she could be deported.
At press time Wednesday, it was not clear what items were removed from Ms. Omar’s home. But witnesses reported seeing boxes labeled “seized property evidence.”
Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said “something’s gonna happen” in the investigation into Ms. Omar’s family’s immigration.
“If we can prove that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place, we’ll deport you,” Secretary Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson.
Even if Ms. Omar’s citizenship status were placed in jeopardy, there would be a long legal process, and she would not face deportation anytime soon, observers say. That means there’s virtually no chance she is deported before the Nov. 3 elections.
As of Oct. 13, at least two of Ms. Omar’s relatives had been subpoenaed in the case, according to news reports.
What other legal issues has Ms. Omar faced?
In 2024, during President Joe Biden’s administration, Ms. Omar faced scrutiny over her personal finances and campaign spending. Her husband, Tim Mynett, is a venture capitalist who has reportedly made millions of dollars from his work. But in April of this year, Ms. Omar revised her estimated assets downward in her required congressional filing, from between $6 million and $30 million to $18,004 to $95,000. No charges of financial fraud have been filed.
But the issue remains live. On Tuesday, Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, said in an interview on Fox News that her office is examining Ms. Omar’s finances.
Ms. Omar has also faced allegations that she married her brother in 2009 to help him secure American citizenship, but there’s no evidence that the man in question, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is her biological brother. They divorced in 2017.
